\chapter{Bastante --- An Ending You Can Already Read}
\label{ch:bastante}
\hlchaptermodality{227}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something is enough, or quite so.}

I can say that something is enough, or quite so.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bastante]{bastante — an ending you can already read}

\label{lesson:ES-C60-bastante}



\begin{quote}
The ending \emph{\textbf{-ante}}, from chapter fifty-two. \emph{Estudiante} — the one who studies. It turns a verb into \emph{the one doing it}.

Keep that in mind; it is about to hand you a word for free.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
There is a verb \emph{\textbf{bastar}}, \emph{to be enough}. Put your ending on it:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{bast-} + \textbf{-ante} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{bastante}}, \textquotedblleft{}sufficing\textquotedblright{}.
\end{quote}

So \emph{bastante} does not mean \emph{a lot}. It means \textbf{enough} — and from there, \emph{quite}, \emph{fairly}. It is the amount that suffices, not the amount that impresses.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Estoy} \emph{\textbf{bastante}} \emph{cansado.} — I'm quite tired.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
You now hold a scale, and it is worth saying out loud in order:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{\textbf{poco}} & little \\
\emph{\textbf{bastante}} & enough, quite \\
\emph{\textbf{muy}} & very \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Notice where \emph{bastante} sits. English speakers reach for it thinking \emph{quite a lot}, and land higher than they meant. It is the middle of the scale, not the top — the top is \emph{muy}.

And unlike \emph{muy}, it is not fussy about what follows: \emph{bastante café}, \emph{bastante grande}. Only \emph{muy} insists on leaning on an adjective or an adverb.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{poco}, \emph{bastante}, \emph{muy}, in order
  \item \emph{Estoy bastante cansado}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \emph{bastante} sit on the scale? (In the \textbf{middle} — enough, not very.)

And which of the three refuses to sit in front of a noun? (\emph{\textbf{Muy}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
